summary: This document proposes a SIP header, Session-ID, that carries a globally unique identifier for a session, kept consistent across proxies, back-to-back user agents and other middleboxes, to help troubleshooting. It documents a mechanism that was already widely deployed. It was replaced by RFC 7989.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone call passes through many switchboards, it helps if every operator writes the same ticket number on it. This RFC adds one shared number so problems can be traced. It was later replaced.

questions: how to trace a sip call across proxies
what is the sip session-id header
how is a sip session-id generated
why do b2buas change the call-id
subtitle: A shared identifier for a SIP session that survives proxies and back-to-back user agents, built for troubleshooting.

tldr.problem: The SIP Call-ID is often changed by back-to-back user agents, so it is hard to follow one session across middleboxes when troubleshooting.
tldr.mechanism: A new Session-ID header carries a 128-bit value, derived from the Call-ID with HMAC-SHA-1 and a secret key and written as 32 lowercase hex characters, which every node must pass along unchanged.
tldr.outcome: It is for troubleshooting only and does not change SIP behavior. The mechanism was widely deployed, and this RFC has been replaced by RFC 7989.

today: RFC 7329 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 7989, which is the Standards Track definition of the idea.

sections.title: Why a Session-ID Is Needed
sections.content:
The SIP Call-ID is a globally unique identifier in every request and response. But Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) and similar middleboxes often change it, and sometimes they must. That makes it hard to tie together the legs of a session on either side of a B2BUA. Proprietary mechanisms were used for this at the time.

This document defines a Session-ID header whose value is not considered unsafe or private, so B2BUAs have no reason to change it. The requirements say it must let administrators correlate dialogs of the same session, must pass through B2BUAs, must not reveal device or domain identity or that the Call-ID was changed, and must not change SIP behavior.

It does not replace the Call-ID and is not used for dialog matching under RFC 3261. The document says it was published as Informational as a reference for later RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switchboard changes the ticket number, so you cannot follow a call. A second number, which nobody has a reason to change, solves that.

sections.title: Generating the Value
sections.content:
The value is the Call-ID hashed with HMAC using SHA-1 (RFC 2104) and a locally generated pseudorandom 128-bit secret key. The 128-bit result is written as lowercase hex, 32 characters. Fixing the algorithm means the format does not reveal the manufacturer, and devices sharing a key can compute the same value.

The secret key means other parties cannot re-create the value. That keeps them from detecting that a Call-ID was changed, which matters because otherwise middleboxes might remove the Session-ID to hide that fact. A generator must remember or re-create the same value for the whole dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is made by scrambling the call's ticket number with a secret. Nobody outside can unscramble it, but the same secret always gives the same number.

sections.title: Behavior of Each Node
sections.content:
A UAC MUST generate a new Session-ID for each out-of-dialog request or new registration, reuse it for in-dialog messages and re-sent requests, and include the header in every message it sends. Registration refreshes MUST reuse the earlier value. A UAS MUST copy the received header into responses and later requests in the dialog, and SHOULD generate one if a request arrives without it.

A Proxy MUST NOT remove or modify the header, MUST copy it to all forked requests and into any response it creates locally, such as 100 Trying. A B2BUA MUST copy it across its two sides and MUST NOT remove, modify or replace a received one. If none arrives, a B2BUA MAY generate one from the received Call-ID.

For transfers, the replacement session reuses the original Session-ID. An out-of-dialog REFER uses the Session-ID of the dialog it targets, a REFER embeds the Session-ID in the Refer-To URI, and an INVITE with Replaces uses the replaced dialog's value if known.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody has a simple rule: if a call arrives with the shared number, copy it onto everything you send, and never change it.

sections.title: The Header and an Example
sections.content:
Session-ID is a single-instance header whose value is exactly 32 characters from 0-9 and a-f, optionally followed by generic parameters. The value is technically case-insensitive, but only lowercase is allowed.

The example in the RFC shows Alice sending an out-of-dialog INVITE that carries a Session-ID. IANA has registered the header field, and the registration is described as temporary until a Standards Track definition is published.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared number is a long string of 32 digits and letters, written in small letters.

sections.title: Migration, Failures and Security
sections.content:
Since SIP is widely deployed, not every device will support Session-ID. Proxies and B2BUAs may generate and insert it for devices that lack support, so adoption can be gradual. The RFC admits Session-ID will sometimes fail to be consistent. For example, with forked requests to unsupporting nodes, each branch may generate a different value, so several appear temporarily.

On security, there is no known issue with viewing or modifying the Session-ID other than hampering troubleshooting. The secret key MUST only be used for this mechanism. Future extensions MUST keep the benign property that gives B2BUAs no reason to interfere, and any header parameters must be registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every switchboard will know the new rule at first, so some can add the number for the others. Sometimes it will not match up, but it still helps most of the time.

data.title: INVITE with a Session-ID header
data.code:
INVITE sip:bob@example.com SIP/2.0
From: Alice <sip:alice@example.net>;tag=1234567
To: Bob <sip:bob@example.com>
Call-Id: 123456mcmxcix@1.2.3.4
Session-ID: f81d4fae7dec11d0a76500a0c91e6bf6
CSeq: 1 INVITE
